With about 2.1% of reports reaching the Top 50, 'a good ladder' alone is not memorable. title: Caplet's distinctive material sits in files judges never read
problem: Judges see 3 notes plus at most 300 words of reflections, a 550-word IPS and the Final Report. The ideas that set Caplet apart (two deposits/two jobs, funder evidence, why-now, price of certainty, real learning stories) are in an 831-page AI record, a 27-page brief and team notes. IPS V5 clearly shows only two of the eight keepers (dated matching; iBonds as dated cash), with the owned floor partly visible. title: 'Each deposit has one job' is the single elegant idea, and V5 does not state it
problem: The case gives two deposits and two goals (case:43-45, 88-92, 101-107). Caplet's design gives each deposit a main job. That is client-driven and easy to remember. V5 describes the sequence (V5:24), but the pitch leads with 'co-sponsors who fund the building rarely pay to run it' (V5:16). That claim is only weakly supported (a US 'starvation cycle' article about overhead), not by evidence that co-sponsors 'rarely' fund operations. The idea only works as a rule: on 15 Oct the holdings basis left $1,372 of room (4.7bp, 0%-carry basis), and about 1 model path in 3 overflows by January. It also needs the 2028 deposit's two parts and the kept half's role settled first.

title: The 'why now' fact survives only on the holdings basis; the team's figures and the case-timing story are stale or false
problem: The team note says the 28 Sep cost was 'the cheapest since May 2002' and that $300k bought all ten on 'only 11% of days since 2000' (notes_and_discussions.md:311-320). Those figures value the old Nov-15 ladder on the trade date. A re-price of every treasury.gov par curve, 3 Jan 2000 to 15 Oct 2026 (6,698 days), gives different answers by basis. Holdings maturities, curve unchanged, valued at 1 Jan 2027: 562 days (8.4%), none from 13 Jul 2007 to 22 Sep 2026. Payment dates: 687 days (10.3%), including one day in Oct 2023 (19 Oct, $299,192), with the first 2026 day on 10 Sep. Either way the true point stands: for most of the last 18 years $300k could not buy all ten payments (2021 median about $427k; peak about $472k on 4 Aug 2020, MODEL). The case-PDF timing story is speculation on any basis.
evidence: team/google_drive/notes_and_discussions.md:173 ('first day in 2026 the ten-payment ladder cost dropped under $300k'), :309-316 ('$289,119, the cheapest since May 2002'; 'Only 11% of days')
verify/L04w/h2.py (verifier re-run): payment-date basis 687 days; 2023-10-19 $299,192; first 2026 day 2026-09-10
fix: If used, the fact goes in the Final Report with its date, its basis and the plan's rule for price changes (a chart only if the 9 Nov instructions allow it). Use a basis-proof wording (rarely affordable since 2008), not 'first time since 2007' or 'since 2002'. The IPS gets at most a clause with no figure. A student rebuilds the figure in a spreadsheet, and the AI help goes in Works Cited. Drop the case-timing story.
deadline: Re-run and log by Sun 15 Nov; Final Report due Sat 5 Dec 09:00 Sydney
verifier_note: hist_ladder.py re-run reproduces 562 days (8.4%), last pre-2026 day 13 Jul 2007, first 2026 day 23 Sep, 2021 median $427,021, peak $472,013. Team's $289,119 is the Nov-15 ladder valued on 28 Sep, not at 1 Jan 2027 (research/insight_v1/verification/ladder_2026-09-28/README.md:3-11), so 'stale' is right. But the fact is basis-sensitive: on the payment-date basis $300k bought all ten on 687 days (10.3%), including 19 Oct 2023 ($299,192), and the first 2026 day was 10 Sep. So 'no day since 2007' holds only on the strict holdings basis, and the case-timing story is not 'false', just speculative (the PDF creation date and any designer intent are UNVERIFIED). A chart in the Final Report is UNVERIFIED until the 9 Nov instructions. Severity high -> medium: this is extra material for the Final Report, and the only real risk is quoting stale or one-basis figures.

title: Co-sponsor communication is the clearest open chance, and Caplet holds verified evidence most teams lack
problem: Creativity now scores communicating 'investment uncertainty clearly and credibly to prospective co-sponsors', a clause new this year. The modal answer will be a percentile band. Five sources re-checked today support a better-designed message: numbers next to probability words; keeping a promise beats exceeding it; seed money signals viability; announcing a lead gift raises giving; one large U.S. capital funder counts only written pledges or cash. Limits: mostly U.S. individual donors or one U.S. foundation, not Taiwanese institutional co-sponsors. Verifier corrections: the Kresge guide is dated 2011 and the challenge grant is now used only 'on occasion'. Its 'committed, imminent or backstopped' test covers named sources only. Budescu's result is that numeric ranges 'increase the correspondence', not that they fix the problem.
evidence: Laura_Gao_2026_Client_Profile.txt:110-120 ('meaningful personal contribution may signal'; 'credible range')
https://www.nature.com/articles/nclimate2194 (accessed 16 Oct 2026): '25 samples in 24 countries and 17 languages' ... 'closer to 50% than intended'
https://www.chicagobooth.edu/review/dont-bother-doing-more-than-you-promised (accessed 16 Oct 2026): 'exceeded promises made them no happier'
https://ideas.repec.org/p/van/wpaper/0008.html (accessed 16 Oct 2026): 'seed money from 10% to 67% ... nearly a sixfold increase'

Kresge guide p.1 (accessed 16 Oct 2026): 'Updated June 30, 2011'; 'Although the challenge grant is no longer the centerpiece of our work, it is used on occasion'
fix: The students' fundraising excerpt must give: a dated, bought bottom; a top set by a stated rule; the chance of reaching the top in words and a number; what bad markets do; and a re-quote rule for the two-year campaign. It must never promise to exceed the top, and it states the evidence's limits. Sources go in the Final Report; the IPS carries only the principle (IPS:68-70, 123-125).

verifier_note: All five quotes found on the live pages (16 Oct 2026). Corrections: the Kresge guide is 'Updated June 30, 2011' and says 'the challenge grant is no longer the centerpiece of our work'. 'Committed, imminent or backstopped' applies only to long-term financing, government funds, organizational funds and bequests, not to all other sources. Budescu: numerical ranges 'increase the correspondence', which is less than 'fixed much'. Gneezy-Epley is cited through a magazine summary, so the Final Report should cite the original paper. Severity stays high: the case requires the fundraising excerpt (case:123-124) and the rubric scores it (deliverables.txt:59).

title: 'About 99%' confidence is circular and looks like everyone's Monte Carlo; the informative number is the chance of reaching the top
problem: The number sheet's 'about 99% (99.4% of 200,000 paths)' is half true by design: the cap stops the gift going above the top. The other half is a real model test of the bottom against coupon shortfalls (IPS_number_sheet.md:17). Quoted as a bare '99 times in 100' ([AI] suggestion 12, IPS_v5_suggestions.md:20), it reads like everyone's Monte Carlo and hides the uncertainty co-sponsors care about: where inside the range the gift lands ('at or within $1,000 of the top in about 3 cases in 4', line 18, MODEL).
fix: The Final Report must still state a confidence, because the case requires one (case:117-118). Explain what makes the top hold (the cap) and what makes the bottom hold (bought Treasuries; the coupon-shortfall test). Add where in the range the gift is likely to land, in words and a number. Rebuild on the holdings basis before quoting. The IPS does not need the range or the figure (IPS:68-70).
deadline: Before the IPS draft, Sat 31 Oct
verifier_note: Number sheet lines 17-18 and suggestion 12 (IPS_v5_suggestions.md:20) verified. Partly wrong: the top cannot be exceeded by design, but the 99.4% is also a real model test of the bottom (the gift falls below it only after a coupon shortfall bigger than the leftover plus Laura's half; sheet line 17). The case requires a confidence statement (case:117-118), so the fix must restate it, not drop it. The final range and co-sponsor text are not expected in the IPS (IPS:68-70), so suggestions 11-12 are optional there.

title: 'Operations pre-funded' is a real funder-facing edge, but V5's pitch over-claims it
problem: V5's pitch says co-sponsors 'rarely pay to run it' (V5:16). The usable lines are Kresge's 2011 question about building 'a larger support base of private giving to address annual operating needs' and the SSIR overhead 'starvation cycle'.

The SSIR 'starvation cycle' (stakeholder_map.md:263-265) gives partial support to the idea that funders underfund running costs.

title: Make '11 trades and hold' read as discipline by logging the decisions not to trade
problem: The Guide and TNA instructions reward 'disciplined decisions' (Guide:181-182; TNA:7). Wharton does not score trade count (Guide:74-77) and discourages frequent trading (faqs.txt:39), so holding is defensible. But the discipline only shows if the checks are logged. The last logged check in the brief is the 14 Oct close. The IBTR note's 'about 0.2 percentage points' was 22.7-23bp of room on 6 Oct and 4.7bp on 15 Oct (same basis), which makes it a genuine 'tested' story if dated.
fix: Keep a dated log of each trigger check and the rule's answer ('hold') through 6 Nov. The IBTR reflection dates its figure to one close. The Final Report shows the log as evidence of discipline.
deadline: Log from Sat 17 Oct; IBTR figure fixed before Tue 20 Oct
verifier_note: Guide:181-182 and TNA:7 ('making disciplined decisions') support the idea. The 22.7bp -> 4.7bp figures are like-for-like (reconcile.py: 6 Oct $293,453 / 23.0bp; 15 Oct 4.7bp). But Wharton says teams are not judged on 'How many trades you make' (Guide:74-77), and the FAQ advises against much buying and selling (faqs.txt:39). So '11 trades reads as passive' is a weak risk. The value of the log is evidence for the IBTR 'tested' story and for Articulation. Severity medium kept because the IBTR dating issue (L05 TNA-01) is due before the TNA.

title: Ladder cost: two honest figures for the same holdings; use the strict one for certainty claims
problem: The 16 Oct sheet's $294k and $5.5k room (IPS_number_sheet.md:12-13) price $50,000 at each 1 Jan payment date with forward rates (ips_numbers.py:87). That equals Caplet's holdings only if the cash from each earlier maturity (2 weeks to 10.5 months early) earns today's forward rates until the payment. The strict figure, where the cash earns nothing and the curve is unchanged, is $298,628, leaving $1,372 (4.7bp; reconcile.py on the 15 Oct close). That strict figure is the same basis as the IBTR note's 6 Oct '$300k is enough unless yields fall about 0.2 points' ($293,453, 23bp then). V5's '$292,000' is the payment-date forward figure; like-for-like it is now about $294.5k. The sheet's '1 case in 3' is anchored to the lower figure (ips_numbers.py:122); on the strict basis the odds are higher. Neither figure counts coupon reinvestment (sheet section 2).
evidence: oct16/research/KB_verify/num/reconcile.py re-run by verifier 16 Oct: payment dates fwd $294,461 / unch $295,246; WInS maturities fwd $297,847 / unch $298,628; 6 Oct WInS unch $293,453 (23.0bp)
fix: For any 'certainty' or 'already bought' claim, and for the IBTR reflection, use the strict figure (about $298.6k, about $1.4k room on 15 Oct), dated, with its assumption named (early cash earns nothing). Use about $294.5k only with its assumption named (early cash earns today's rates). Prefer no dollar figure in the IPS (IPS:51-52; oct14/final.md objective 8). If suggestion 5 is kept, it must name its date and assumption.
deadline: Before the IBTR reflection, Tue 20 Oct
verifier_note: Numbers reproduce exactly (reconcile.py: $294,461 / $295,246 / $297,847 / $298,628) and ips_numbers.py:87 prices to dt.date(y,1,1), with :122 anchoring the odds to that figure. But the interpretation is wrong. $294.5k is not 'a ladder Caplet cannot own': it is Caplet's own holdings if the cash from each early maturity earns today's forward rates until the payment date. $298.6k assumes that cash earns 0% and the curve is unchanged. So the gap is a reinvestment assumption, not ownership. Both figures are zero-coupon views and ignore coupon reinvestment.

title: The co-sponsor research Caplet calls its 'most original part' misreads its key funder source
